title: Fix SSE escape/trailer corruption during interleaved function-call streaming
author: Mariana Cortez
release_notes: Fixes rare stream corruption that could cause partial JSON fragments to be emitted during function/tool-call handoff, improving streaming stability and OpenAI-compat behavior.
description:
Summary: Fix a class of SSE streaming failures where an escape-like trailing byte sequence emitted at the end of a function/tool-call payload could be misinterpreted by the streaming lexer and produce truncated or syntactically invalid JSON frames for downstream OpenAI-compatible clients. This manifested as malformed partial JSON in long-running streaming responses, most often when the user-supplied tool payload ended with '\\' or when the runtime emitted a delimiter immediately after a binary/base64-encoded chunk.

Motivation: Customers reported intermittent errors during streaming tool calls where the client-side JSON parser would raise a parse error halfway through a function-call boundary. Root cause analysis showed the streaming FSM would sometimes drop a delimiter or fold a trailing escape into the following 'data:' line when fragments arrived in edge-sized TCP packets or when backpressure caused interleaving between model tokens and tool payload flushes.

Root cause: The sse stream lexer assumed delimiters ("\n\n" or a full 'data: ' event line) were always emitted atomically. In cases where the last byte of a payload looked like an escape/escape-like byte sequence (e.g. trailing backslash, CR without LF, or base64 chunk break), the lexer would transition into an escape-state that incorrectly consumed the next event's leading bytes as part of the payload rather than boundary markers. This was exacerbated when function-call sentinel markers (tool boundaries) were emitted back-to-back.

This change:
- Rework the small-state streaming lexer to introduce a "trailer buffer" that conservatively holds up to 8 bytes when a potential escape/trailer is detected. The buffer is validated against delimiter patterns before committing bytes to the active JSON span.
- Add an explicit handoff path for function/tool-call sentinel emission: when transitioning from token stream -> tool payload -> token stream, the emitter now inserts an idempotent sentinel marker with a hint header (x-sse-sentinel: toolcall) that the lexer recognizes to force boundary secures even if fragments split across packets.
- Normalize emitter behavior for trailing CR/\n and stray backslashes so the client-visible 'data:' lines are never produced in a way that can be stitched into the adjacent event.
- Tighten timeout-rescue semantics: if the trailer buffer doesn't resolve within 120ms (configurable) the lexer emits a safe-rescue marker and continues rather than stalling the stream. This trades a deterministic small marker for availability and avoids client-side hangs during network pathologies.
- Add integration tests that simulate packetized fragment arrival, deliberate backpressure, and tool payloads ending in escape-like bytes.

Files changed (high level):
- go/protocol/sse/stream_lexer.go — new trailer buffer and state transitions.
- go/protocol/sse/emitter.go — sentinel header injection and normalization of trailing bytes.
- go/protocol/sse/lexer_test.go — expanded unit tests including fuzz harness for edge packets.
- node/openai-compat/stream-adapter.ts — compatibility guard for idempotent sentinel markers and fallback parsing.
- integration/tests/toolcall_stream_fragments.yaml — end-to-end scenarios simulating interleaved fragments and delayed delimiters.
- docs/api/sse-boundaries.md — documented the new sentinel header and rescue behavior for users integrating low-level streaming clients.

Checklist: 
- [x] Reproduce issue deterministically in integration harness.
- [x] Fix lexer state machine and add unit+integration tests.
- [x] Add emitter-side guard to prevent ambiguous trailer emission.
- [x] Update OpenAI-compat adapter to accept sentinel hints.
- [x] Performance: ensure no measurable token-latency regression (microbench shows <0.5% median increase).
- [x] Security review (no new unsafe parsers or unbounded buffering).

Testing & QA:
- Unit tests added for deterministic fragment sequences (packet sizes: 5–64 bytes).
- Fuzz harness extended to generate boundary cases for trailing backslashes, CR-only endings, and base64 line-break placements.
- Integration E2E runs in CI that replay recorded incidents from SUP-2187 and validate stream JSON roundtrip for both native Redwood clients and the OpenAI-compat adapter.
- Canary rollout: behind feature-flag 'sse-trailer-buffer', staged to 10% of traffic for 48 hours before global flip.

Rollout plan: Merge to main, deploy emitter + lexer updates together as an atomic runtime release. Feature flag controls rescue timeout and may be dialed down while monitoring. Observe streaming-error-rate, client-parse-failures, and per-route latency.

Related: SUP-2187 incident report, ENG-4921 (streaming robustness epic), small followup planned to expose rescue-timeout to Dedicated configs.

Notes: This PR intentionally prefers conservative buffering and explicit sentinel markers over heuristics that guessed at delimiter boundaries. The approach reduces rare parse failures at the cost of a tiny deterministic marker in the pathological path and a small, bounded buffer on the lexer side.

review_comments: Owen Patel: Could you clarify why we need the 8-byte limit for the trailer buffer? Is it empirically chosen or arbitrary?

Mariana Cortez: 8 bytes came from histogram of observed trailer lengths in production traces; it covers >99.9% of cases and keeps memory bounded. Added comment and unit test to show behavior when exceeded.
Lena Fischer: Unit tests look good. I requested an additional integration test for back-to-back toolcall sentinel emission — can we add that?
Mariana Cortez: Added back-to-back sentinel integration case and a check that emitter doesn't duplicate sentinel when the previous token stream already supplied one.
Dylan Reed: Lint flagged a small naming issue; fixed in last commit. Performance microbench shows 0.3% median token latency increase — acceptable.
Owen Patel: Approving after reading docs; this looks safe and the rescue behavior is sane.
